source: Ark, Brooks, Eva (2006) Giving learners the best of both worlds: teaching pattern recognition to novices
finding: Novices told to use both feature-first and similarity-based strategies diagnosed ECGs better than those told to use either one alone. Supports an additive model.
numbers: N=48 McMaster psychology undergraduates, 12 per group, 10 cardiac diagnoses. Feature-first 42%, first-impression 41% (p>.4). Explicit combined 56%, implicit combined 53% (both p<.01).
quote: the groups instructed to use both strategies (explicitly or implicitly) performed significantly better (56% and 53%, respectively; p < .01)
limits: Abstract read on Europe PMC; full text not open. Tiny groups, laboratory ECG task, undergraduates not doctors, one lab. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Test an agent that gets both a feature checklist (script) and a similar solved case. Compare with either alone at equal tokens. Gap 2 is still untested for LLMs.

source: Schmidt, Boshuizen (1993) On the origin of intermediate effects in clinical case recall
finding: Two experiments. Intermediate-level students recalled more of a case than experts and novices. The effect vanished when study time was cut, and it was produced experimentally by priming pathophysiology knowledge.
numbers: Two experiments (Experiment 1: free recall by level of expertise with restricted study time; Experiment 2: priming for short vs longer time). Cell sizes and effect sizes are not in the abstract.
quote: Experts use knowledge in an encapsulated mode while comprehending a case, whereas students use elaborated knowledge.
limits: Abstract only. Sample sizes could not be recovered (paper is paywalled). The original claim rests on a small number of cases and subjects per level.
agent_relevance: Intermediate effect is time- and instruction-dependent. For an LLM the analogue is that forced elaboration changes what is reported, not what is concluded.

source: van de Wiel, Schmidt, Boshuizen (1998) A failure to reproduce the intermediate effect in clinical case recall
finding: Failed replication by the original group. Recall rose in a straight line with expertise. Experts recalled more because they elaborated more. Constraining time hurt recall at all levels.
numbers: Second-, fourth- and sixth-year students plus internists; 4 internal medicine cases; study time 3 min, 1 min 15 s or 30 s. Diagnostic accuracy rose with expertise.
quote: this study failed to disclose the intermediate effect in clinical case recall that was found in the original study
limits: Abstract only; group sizes not in the abstract. The authors conclude experts can use either the encapsulated or the elaborated mode.
agent_relevance: The intermediate effect is not a fixed law. Do not build an agent rule on it. Treat detail level as a switchable mode.

source: Rikers, Schmidt, Boshuizen (2000) Knowledge encapsulation and the intermediate effect
finding: Neurologists and 2nd- and 6th-year students diagnosed cardiology and pulmonology cases outside the neurologists' field. Recall showed an inverted U, and the share of encapsulating concepts rose with expertise.
numbers: Neurologists vs 2nd-year vs 6th-year students; 4 cases (2 cardiology, 2 pulmonology). Neurologists faster and more accurate. 6th-year students recalled most. Group sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Companion study Rikers 2002 (cardiologists vs pulmonologists, 4 cases) found no qualitative difference in recall or explanations when cases were outside the specialty.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that encapsulation is a general processing mode, not a topic-specific store. Weak input to design.

source: Wimmers, Schmidt, Verkoeijen, van de Wiel (2005) Inducing expertise effects in clinical case recall
finding: Expert nephrologists, intermediate students and novices saw 6 cases in 3 conditions. An expertise effect on recall appeared only when people had to elaborate on each finding. With history and exam context the intermediate effect appeared.
numbers: 6 cases, 3 conditions (lab data only; lab data with elaboration instruction; lab data with clinical context). Elaboration instruction changed only the experts' recall.
quote: expertise effects in clinical case recall are only produced when the normal processing of patient information is disrupted
limits: Abstract only; sample sizes not in the abstract. One specialty (nephrology).
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the human intermediate effect depends on whether elaboration is forced. The same variable can be set for an LLM (list all findings vs conclude).

source: Eberhard, Klomp, Foge, Hedderich, Schmidt (2009) The intermediate effect in dental medicine
finding: An intermediate effect was seen in dentistry: fifth-year students wrote more recall than third- and fourth-year students and experts. Diagnostic accuracy rose with experience.
numbers: 61 students and 20 specialised dentists; 3 cases; interrater agreement 96.2 +/- 3.37%; diagnostic accuracy trend p<0.001; fifth-year recall higher (Games-Howell, p<0.05).
limits: Abstract only. One domain and one school. Shows the effect can replicate in another field, against van de Wiel 1998 which did not.
agent_relevance: Evidence is split (2 for, 1 against, plus conditions). Keep K02 as contested.

source: Norman, Brooks (1997) The non-analytical basis of clinical reasoning
finding: Several McMaster studies argue that diagnosis uses similarity to specific past cases. Experts err on typical cases as often as novices. A positive history changed what was seen on films.
numbers: Dermatology: specific similarity explains about 30% of diagnosis. About 40% of errors by residents, GPs and dermatologists were on typical slides. Radiology: positive history raised features seen by about 50%. Experts predicted only 11-60% of colleagues' errors.
quote: specific similarity accounts for about 30% of diagnosis
limits: Abstract only. Figures are from the paper's summary, not checked in the full text. Lab-style slide tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 background: exemplar similarity is a separate source of signal from the script. Also shows a stated hypothesis re-interprets findings (anchoring in humans).

source: Norman, Young, Brooks (2007) Non-analytical models of clinical reasoning: the role of experience
finding: Review of the McMaster programme. Non-analytic reasoning appears at all levels in dermatology, ECG and psychiatry. Retrieval is fast and not open to introspection. Early hypotheses can lead to re-interpretation of findings.
numbers: No pooled numbers given in the abstract.
quote: Non-analytic reasoning is a central component of diagnostic expertise at all levels.
limits: Abstract only. Written by the same group whose studies it reviews.
agent_relevance: Teach an agent both: multiple stored examples plus an analytic de-biasing step. This matches the Ark 2006 result.

source: Sibbald, McKinney, Cavalcanti, Yu, Wood, Nair, Eva, Hatala (2013) Cardiac examination and dual-processing instruction
finding: Randomised trials in three groups (experienced, intermediate, novice). Telling people to use dual-processing (analytic check after an initial impression) did not change the probability assigned to the correct diagnosis.
numbers: Three experiments on a cardiopulmonary simulator, each randomised to undirected vs dual-processing instruction. No effect on the probability of the correct diagnosis in any of the three.
quote: dual-processing instruction did not change the probability assigned to the correct diagnosis in any of the three experiments
limits: Abstract read. Cardiac auscultation, not text vignettes. Group sizes not recovered here.
agent_relevance: Human parallel to Savage 2024 (clinician-style prompts did not help GPT-4): instruction to reason in a clinician style does not by itself raise accuracy. Gap 3 partial.

source: Keemink, Custers, van Dijk, ten Cate (2018) Illness script development in pre-clinical education
finding: After a case-based reasoning course, pre-clinical students had richer scripts and better diagnosis for course diseases. Exam score tracked recognition, not script richness.
numbers: N=32, within subject. Script richness 14.47 (SD 3.25) vs 12.14 (SD 2.80), p<0.001 (about 20% higher). More enabling-condition content. Diagnostic score 1.63 vs 1.15, p<0.001. Exam vs recognition r=0.571; exam vs richness r=-0.006.
quote: illness script richness for CBCR diseases was almost 20% higher than for non-CBCR diseases
limits: Disease-specific, not general. Small N, one course. Script richness did not track exam score.
agent_relevance: Supports K07 (enabling conditions) but warns that richer script text is not the same as better diagnosis. Gap 8: a count of script features is a weak proxy for skill.

source: Yanagita, Yokokawa, Fukuzawa, Uchida, Uehara, Ikusaka (2024) Expert assessment of ChatGPT's ability to generate illness scripts (full text)
finding: GPT-4 scripts were weakest in cardiovascular and psychiatric systems. The text says the scripts ignored how frequent a symptom is and how sensitive a test is.
numbers: 184 diseases, 16 areas, 3 physician raters. Overall A 56.0%, B 28.3%, C 15.8%. Cardiovascular: 6 of 14 rated C (42.9%). Psychiatric: 5 of 11 rated C (45.5%). Dermatological 0 of 13 C; respiratory 0 of 11 C; gastrointestinal 1 of 25 C. Example error: droplet transmission listed for varicella.
quote: the compilation of symptoms and tests did not consider the frequency of symptoms or the sensitivity of the tests
limits: Single model, one prompt style with character limits, Japanese curriculum list, no retrieval arm. Small cells per area (2 to 25). Gap 4 field question answered; the retrieval fix was not tested.
agent_relevance: A self-written class library is least reliable where criteria are graded (doses by size, DSM criteria) and where numeric weight is needed. Verify these fields or fill from a checked source. No frequency or sensitivity fields were produced: add them.

source: Avnat et al. (2025) Numerical vs semantic medical knowledge: benchmarking on evidence-based Q&As (EBMQA)
finding: Two frontier LLMs did better on semantic questions (which entity differs) than on numeric ones (how strongly a finding relates to a disease). Both lagged doctors on the numeric questions.
numbers: 24,542 QAs analysed from 105,222 built from a knowledge graph. Semantic: Claude 3 Opus 68.7%, GPT-4 68.4%. Numeric: 63.7% and 56.7% (Claude better, p<.001). On 100 numeric questions six experts scored 82.3% vs Claude 64.3% and GPT-4 55.8% (both p<.001).
quote: Both LLMs excelled more in semantic than numerical QAs
limits: 2024 models (GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus). Newer models not tested. Questions come from one knowledge graph. Expert test used only 6 doctors.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the numeric side of a script (how much a finding or setting should shift belief) is the weak part of LLM knowledge. A graded prior must be supplied by the scaffold, not trusted from the model.

source: Feng et al. (2026) Evidence-Value Misalignment in dynamic medical diagnosis (MedEVM, EVD-Harness with Contrastive Diagnostic Wiki)
finding: Closest study to gap 1. A stored wiki of confusable disease pairs with their distinguishing findings (built from case reports, checked against source passages) lifted accuracy over no knowledge, random pages and plain BM25 pages. The harness also adds a review step.
numbers: 1,050 cases, 24 disease systems, 9 LLMs tested, harness on 5. Gains 12.0 to 51.1 points over the plain LLM. Ablation on 200 cases: removing the wiki cut accuracy 9.0 to 14.5 points; removing the evidence witness cut 3.5 to 9.0. Qwen3.8-27B: none 63.0, random 64.0, BM25 67.0, contrastive 72.0, full wiki 75.5.
quote: Removing it while retaining CDW lowers accuracy by 3.5-9.0 points.
limits: Preprint by one lab. Compares wiki against no wiki, not against the same tokens spent on free chain of thought. Mixed with a review module, so the wiki effect is not isolated from the harness. Cases are published case reports, so prevalence is not representative. Task is submit-or-wait diagnosis, not NEJM differentials.
agent_relevance: Strong direct support that a verified, contrast-organised class library helps, and that structure (contrast pairs) beats raw retrieval. Still no equal-token test against free CoT.

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Einstellung effect in medical LLMs; ECR-Agent
finding: Counterfactual pairs show strong LLMs lock onto the common diagnosis and miss the one finding that flips it. An agent with causal-graph reasoning plus a stored exemplar base and evolving illness graphs reduced the effect.
numbers: 5,383 paired cases, 49 diseases, 17 LLMs. Bias trap rate for frontier models above 50% (Gemini-2.5-Pro 60.90%, GPT-5 51.87%). ECR-Agent on Qwen3-32B: baseline accuracy 40.25 to 55.49 (causal module) to 69.49 (plus exemplar base and illness graphs); trap rate 43.46 to 38.32 to 33.75. Debate-style agents MDAgent 40.34% and DyLAN 41.69% trap rates.
quote: no meaningful correlation exists between model size and robustness
limits: Benchmark and fix come from the same authors; code not yet released. Ablation does not separate exemplars from illness graphs, so gap 2 is not answered. Only 49 common diseases. Table text partly garbled in the PDF extraction.
agent_relevance: Shows exemplar-plus-script memory helps on a hard counterfactual set, and that role-debate did not. Also shows stronger models are more anchored, which matters for gap 6.

source: Adewuyi et al. (2026) MamaBench: counterfactual benchmark, Evidence-Anchored RAG
finding: Retrieval from a verified clinical reference helps only a little unless it is built to cover discriminating parameters. Plain top-k retrieval did not reduce failures on paired cases.
numbers: 217 pairs, 371 pathologies, 8 configurations. Bias trap rate: Claude Sonnet 4.6 alone 25.8% to EA-RAG 20.3%, robust accuracy 60.8 to 65.0, base accuracy 82.0 to 81.6. GPT-4o: RAG baseline 39.9%, EA-RAG 35.9%. Base accuracy overstates robust accuracy by 16 to 28 points.
quote: Vanilla RAG does not help.
limits: Maternal and paediatric domain, 434 narratives, one lab. No GPT-4o no-retrieval arm, so the effect of plain RAG is not separated. Retrieval corpus is textbooks and WHO guidance, not scripts.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partial: retrieving from a verified source cut the failure rate by 4.0 to 5.5 points only, and about 1 in 5 pairs still failed. A verified library is not a full fix.

source: ER-Reason authors (2025/2026) ER-Reason: LLM reasoning across the emergency workflow with SCT-style belief updating
finding: On real ER records, reasoning models did not beat non-reasoning ones at updating belief, and accuracy fell as evidence piled up. Physician rationales that explain why a finding shifts the differential raised accuracy for every model.
numbers: 25,174 notes, 3,437 patients; 194 SCT cases, 787 items, 2,555 annotations. Final-diagnosis ICD-10 exact match best 39.91% zero-shot. GPT-5.2 Thinking vs GPT-5.2: DxUpdate p=0.455, DxTrajectory p=0.192. Claude 4.5 Thinking below its base on DxTrajectory (difference 0.044, p<0.001). DxUpdate zero-shot about 0.54 (Phi-4) to 0.69 (o4-mini), rising to about 0.69-0.81 with oracle rationales.
quote: We did not find inference-time chain-of-thought to provide benefit on sequential belief updating
limits: Preprint. Oracle rationales may just point attention to the right hypothesis. The paper does not report how well SCT scores predict final-diagnosis accuracy, so gap 8 is not closed.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and gap 3: SCT-style belief updating exposes a weakness that more thinking does not fix. Expert-written text on why this finding shifts the differential is a useful class-library field.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of LLMs in agentic clinical reasoning (OncoRounds)
finding: Across 32 models, the best reached 68.1%. Information use was the strongest predictor of accuracy. Reasoning traces scored well but did not track correctness. Anchoring, premature closure and search satisficing were the main errors.
numbers: 20 hematology cases, 3 rounds. Mean accuracy 56.3% (SD 7.4). Differential reasoning weakest at 43.6% vs diagnosis 66.6%. Of 323 wrong or partial first diagnoses, 65.6% stayed wrong by round 3; of 307 correct, 50.8% got worse. Utilisation 56.8% in R1 to 25.7% in R3. R-IDEA rubric: 91.1% of traces at or above 6/10, correlation with accuracy only R=0.56, outlier GPT-OSS 120B 56.4% accuracy with rubric 8.90.
quote: the primary limitation of current models in clinical oncology is not insufficient medical knowledge but a systematic failure of information-seeking under uncertainty
limits: 20 cases, one specialty, LLM judge checked against one hematologist. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 indirect: more reasoning text did not mean better ranking. Gap 9: the failure is early commitment, so a challenger step has to act at the first hypothesis, not at the end.

source: You et al. (2026) Improving clinical diagnosis with counterfactual multi-agent reasoning
finding: A challenger-style method that edits findings and watches how confidence in each diagnosis moves beat zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, self-consistency and three published multi-agent systems. Gains were largest for weak models and hard cases.
numbers: 3 datasets (MIMIC-CDM-FI, MedCaseReasoning, ER-Reason), 7 LLMs. Llama-3.1-8B average 39.0% (+13.2 over zero-shot CoT); m1 only +2.2. DeepSeek-R1: beat second-best (few-shot CoT) by 4.1%. On ER-Reason few-shot CoT (14.0%) was below zero-shot CoT (16.7%) for DeepSeek.
quote: few-shot CoT (14.0%) underperforms zero-shot CoT (16.7%)
limits: Preprint; baselines are other groups' methods, so partly independent. No equal-token comparison reported in the text read. Small open models, exact-match labels.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a structured challenger can add accuracy, mostly for weak models and hard cases. Gap 2: fixed 5-shot examples were the strongest simple baseline for DeepSeek but hurt it on ER-Reason.

source: Xia et al. (2026) Structured Debate-Mixture-of-Agents (DMoA) for complex diagnosis
finding: Most of the gain over one model came from running several proposers. Adding a rebuttal stage added only about 1 to 1.5 points. More tokens helped.
numbers: 297 rare-disease cases and 1,719 challenging cases. GPT-4o challenging cases top-1: single 14.50%, 4x1 mixture 23.98%, full 4x2 DMoA 25.34% (rare disease: 28.62, 32.66, 35.20). Whole-set gain over GPT-4o: +10.21 points top-1. Token budget 16,000 to 4,000 cut rare-disease top-1 from 35.20% to 30.98%. Removing the Rebutter lowered GPT-4o top-1 (25.26% vs 26.79% in the full model).
quote: gain of DMoA cannot be explained by prompt design alone
limits: Preprint, GPT-4o era models, one team. Ablations vary structure but not strictly equal total tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a rebuttal role is a small part of the gain. Sampling several independent proposals does most of the work. Check any challenger step against plain voting at equal cost.

source: Duke-NUS group (2024) Enhancing diagnostic accuracy through multi-agent conversations to mitigate cognitive bias
finding: Four GPT-4 agents (diagnoser, devil's advocate, facilitator, recorder) discussed 16 case reports of known bias-caused misdiagnoses. No single-agent control was run.
numbers: 16 cases, 80 simulations. Initial diagnosis 0/80 correct by design; after discussion top differential 57/80 (71.3%), top two 64/80 (80.0%).
quote: the initial diagnosis had an accuracy of 0% (0/80)
limits: No baseline: a plain GPT-4 asked the same question was not scored, and cases were selected for misdiagnosis. Cannot show that the devil's advocate caused the gain. Case reports likely in training data.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: this study cannot answer it. Do not cite 71.3% as an effect of a challenger role.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (BiasMedQA), mitigation tables
finding: Bias education, one-shot and few-shot bias demonstrations recovered part of the loss for GPT-4 but little for other models. No devil's-advocate or challenger arm was tested.
numbers: 1,273 questions, 7 biases. GPT-4 unbiased 72.7%. Education: frequency bias 0.627 to 0.720. One-shot: recency 0.679 to 0.742. Few-shot: GPT-4 recency 0.764 and status quo 0.770 (table values). Average loss across models: false consensus 24.9, frequency 18.2, recency 12.9, confirmation 8.1 points.
quote: gpt-4 consistently shows the highest level of improvement across all strategies
limits: 2023-era models. Single-letter answers with no reasoning allowed. Table layout in the PDF extraction was hard to read, so some per-cell values are uncertain. The preprint's 'GPT-3.5 average drop 37.4%' is not reliable (see critique).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 9: prompting about biases helps strong models a little, weak models almost not. Equal-token comparison to a challenger step is missing.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) MedAgentBoard: multi-agent collaboration vs single LLMs and conventional methods
finding: An independent benchmark found multi-agent collaboration did not consistently beat a strong single LLM on text medical QA. Self-consistency was the most expensive single-LLM option, more costly than the multi-agent systems.
numbers: 4 task families. MedQA multiple choice best score 89.90% (CoT-SC, single LLM). MedAgents 83.85% on PubMedQA multiple choice. DeepSeek-V3 zero-shot 91.23% on PubMedQA free-form (LLM judge).
quote: it does not consistently outperform advanced single LLMs
limits: Not a diagnosis-from-case task. Models are from 2025 and the study does not test MAI-DxO. Does not test equal-token matching directly.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partial: independent evidence that role scaffolds do not carry across tasks automatically. MAI-DxO itself has still not been re-run by a third party in what I could find.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Benchmarking multi-turn medical diagnosis: Hold, Lure, and Self-Correction (MINT)
finding: Models commit to an answer early. Salient lab results trigger premature answers even when told to wait. Models do correct themselves, and wrong-to-right revisions greatly outnumber right-to-wrong.
numbers: 1,035 cases, 11 LLMs. Over 55% of answers committed in the first two turns. Wrong-to-right revisions up to 10.6 times as common as right-to-wrong. Deferring the diagnostic question raised accuracy at first commitment by up to 62.6%; holding back salient evidence avoided a drop of up to 23.3%.
quote: models rush to answer before sufficient evidence has been observed
limits: Abstract and front matter read; body not examined in detail. Preprint. Cases split into evidence shards by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and 9: early commitment is the weak point, and a late-asking or hold step is cheap. This favours 'list hypotheses first, answer last' over elaborating early.

source: Noever (2024) Language models and a second opinion use case: the pocket professional
finding: On 183 hard Medscape cases models scored high against the crowd answer on easy cases and far lower on contested ones.
numbers: 183 cases over 20 months. Overall above 80% for the newest models; straightforward cases above 81%; complex cases 43%. 21 Supreme Court cases as a second set.
quote: performance disparity between straightforward cases (>81% accuracy) and complex scenarios (43% accuracy)
limits: Abstract and intro read. Reference is the crowd majority, which is not ground truth. One author, 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: any clinician-style prompt test must be split by case difficulty, since overall accuracy hides a drop on hard cases.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in LLM systems for rare disease diagnosis
finding: Retrieval or agent systems reported high rare-disease accuracy partly through leakage. Strict cross-dataset isolation cut accuracy a lot.
numbers: Over 60,000 cases. Cross-dataset mean Recall@1 fell from 54.3% to 40.3% (Hedges g=0.94). Supervised classifier accuracy fell from 42.9% to 16.7% (Cohen d=2.01).
quote: prevailing evaluation protocols for augmented LLM systems inadvertently reflect data leakage rather than genuine medical reasoning
limits: Rare disease phenotype data, not NEJM text. Preprint. Abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 caution: gains from knowledge-augmented or agent systems, including vendor ones, should be re-measured on cases that are not in the library or the training set.
